Bray
BRAY
verb
Two distinct words fell together in English. The first is from the Old French braire, to cry out, used of the ass’s harsh call. The second is from the Old French breier, to pound or crush small, used of grinding in a mortar. The Authorized Version employs both, and each carries its own lesson.

Biblical Definition

The first bray is the cry of a beast in want. “Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass?” (Job 6:5) — Job’s defence of his own complaining. The animal does not cry when it is fed; its noise is the honest evidence of an empty belly, and Job means that his groaning is likewise not petulance but the sound of real affliction. Scripture does not despise the cry of the sufferer, and it does not require the afflicted to pretend contentment they have not been given. The second bray is the work of the mortar, and it yields one of the bleakest verses in Proverbs: “Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him” (Pro 27:22). Grain is pounded to separate the husk from the kernel; the process works because the husk is not the grain. But pound a fool and you get a bruised fool, because his folly is not a husk clinging to him — it is his kernel. This is a doctrine of the heart, not a proverb about stubborn personalities. Affliction of itself sanctifies nobody. Pressure removes what is external; only regeneration changes what a man is. Two brayings, then: the honest cry of the hungry, and the useless pounding of the fool.

Webster 1828 Definition

To utter a harsh cry, as an ass; and, from a distinct root, to pound or grind small in a mortar. Both senses stand in the Authorized Version.

expand to see more

BRAY, v.i. To utter a harsh, loud cry, as an ass; hence, to make any harsh, disagreeable noise.

From the Old French braire, to cry out.

BRAY, v.t. To pound, beat, or grind small, as in a mortar with a pestle.

From the Old French breier, to break or pound; a distinct word accidentally alike in form.

Pro 27:22 employs the second sense: to bray a fool in a mortar is to pound him small.

Key Scripture

Job 6:5 — "Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder?"

Pro 27:22 — "Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, yet will not his foolishness depart from him."

Job 30:7 — "Among the bushes they brayed; under the nettles they were gathered together."

Jer 6:29 — "The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire ; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away."

Modern Corruption

The modern faith that hardship automatically produces character is exactly the error Pro 27:22 was written to destroy — the mortar does not convert the fool.

expand to see more

The corruption is the doctrine of redemptive suffering without redemption. It is now a commonplace that difficulty builds people, that adversity is the universal teacher, that what does not destroy a man makes him stronger. Scripture flatly contradicts this as a general rule. Pharaoh was pounded with ten plagues and came out harder each time. Ahaz, in the time of his distress, did trespass yet more against the LORD — and the chronicler adds the terrible words this is that king Ahaz. The mortar is real, the pestle is real, and the fool comes out the other side a fool, only bruised. Suffering is not a sacrament; it does not work by the doing of the work.

Recover the plain sense: affliction is a means God uses, but it is not a mechanism that runs by itself, and its effect depends entirely on whether the Spirit attends it. The same furnace that softens wax hardens clay. Where God is pleased to sanctify a trouble, it purges dross and yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to them which are exercised thereby — note exercised, a word of active submission, not passive endurance. Where He is not, the same trouble produces only bitterness and a harder heart. So do not tell the afflicted that their pain will automatically improve them, and do not despise their crying: Job 6:5 grants the wild ass its bray.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Two roots, one spelling: Old French braire, to cry out, and breier, to pound small — the cry of want and the useless pounding of folly.

expand to see more

Bray (1) — Old French braire, to cry harshly, as an ass (Job 6:5).

Bray (2) — Old French breier, to pound or grind in a mortar (Pro 27:22).

The two words are unrelated in origin and fell together in English form.

The mortar separates husk from kernel — which is why it fails on a fool.

Job 6:5 defends the honesty of the sufferer’s cry.

Usage

"Job 6:5: the beast cries only when it lacks — the groan is evidence, not petulance."

"Pro 27:22 denies that affliction of itself removes folly; the folly is the kernel, not the husk."

"Distinguish the two words: one is a noise, the other a grinding."
